questions.q: What are the three standard orthographic views used to represent a 3D solid on paper?
questions.a: The three standard views are the front view, top view, and side view. A wrong answer (e.g., "isometric, oblique, perspective") reveals the student confuses orthographic projection with pictorial drawing methods and does not recall the specific terminology for the three principal views.

questions.q: Why does a right circular cylinder standing on its base have a rectangular front view but a circular top view?
questions.a: From the front, you see the cylinder's height and diameter, which form a rectangle; from the top, you look down onto the circular base, so you see a circle. A wrong answer (e.g., "both are circles") shows the student does not understand that the view depends on the direction of projection and the orientation of the solid.

questions.q: A solid is made by stacking two identical cubes of side 3 cm one on top of the other. Draw the front, top, and side views (describe the shape and dimensions of each view).
questions.a: Front view: rectangle 3 cm wide × 6 cm high. Top view: square 3 cm × 3 cm. Side view: rectangle 3 cm wide × 6 cm high. Steps: 1) The stack has total height 6 cm, width 3 cm, depth 3 cm. 2) Front view shows height and width → 3×6 rectangle. 3) Top view shows width and depth → 3×3 square. 4) Side view shows height and depth → 3×6 rectangle. A wrong answer (e.g., top view as 3×6 rectangle) reveals the student cannot mentally separate the dimensions that each view captures.

questions.q: Compare the front view of a right circular cone (base on table) and a square pyramid (base on table). How are they similar and how do they differ?
questions.a: Both front views are triangles (the cone's triangle has a curved base line if the cone is oblique, but for a right cone it is a straight line; the pyramid's triangle has a straight base). They are similar in overall triangular shape. They differ in the top view: the cone's top view is a circle, the pyramid's top view is a square. A wrong answer (e.g., "both front views are rectangles") shows the student cannot visualize the outline of a cone or pyramid from the front.

questions.q: A student says: "The front view is a 4 cm × 4 cm square, the top view is a 4 cm × 4 cm square, and the side view is a 4 cm × 4 cm square. Therefore the solid must be a cube of side 4 cm." Is the student correct? Justify your answer.
questions.a: The student is not necessarily correct. A cuboid with dimensions 4 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm (a cube) gives those views, but so does any solid that fits inside a 4 cm cube and has the same silhouette from all three directions (e.g., a sphere of diameter 4 cm, or a cylinder of diameter 4 cm and height 4 cm). The three views alone do not guarantee the solid is a cube. A wrong answer (e.g., "Yes, it must be a cube") reveals the student thinks orthographic views uniquely determine the solid, ignoring that different solids can share the same projections.

questions.q: Design a solid using exactly four unit cubes such that its front view is an L-shape, its top view is a 2×2 square, and its side view is a 2×2 square. Describe the arrangement of the cubes.
questions.a: Place three cubes on the bottom layer forming an L (two cubes side by side along the x-axis, and one cube attached to the left cube along the y-axis). Place the fourth cube on top of the cube at the corner of the L (the one that has two neighbours). This gives a top view of a 2×2 square (the bottom layer covers three of the four cells, the top cube covers the fourth cell from above). The front view (looking along the y-axis) shows an L-shape 2 cubes high and 2 cubes wide. The side view (looking along the x-axis) also shows a 2×2 square because the top cube fills the missing column. A poor answer (e.g., random arrangement) reveals the student cannot work backwards from views to a 3D configuration.
